**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Further Mathematics Paper 2 (0775), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2023. Time allowed: three hours.**

Answer ALL 10 questions. For your guidance, the approximate mark allocation for parts of each question is indicated. Mathematical formulae and tables published by the Board, and noiseless non-programmable electronic calculators are allowed. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Show that the set of matrices of the form
$$\begin{pmatrix} x & y \\ -y & x \end{pmatrix}, \quad\text{where } x \neq 0, \text{ and } x, y \in \mathbb{R},$$
forms a group under matrix multiplication. (*Assume Associativity*). (5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Write $S = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} x & y \\ -y & x \end{pmatrix} : x, y \in \mathbb{R} \right\}$ and let $G$ be the subset of those matrices that are **invertible**, i.e. with $\det = x^{2} + y^{2} \neq 0$, equivalently $(x, y) \neq (0, 0)$.

**A necessary remark on the condition printed in the question.** With the restriction $x \neq 0$ alone the set is *not* closed under multiplication. For example $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ has $x = 1 \neq 0$, but
$$A^{2} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$$
has top-left entry $0$. So the statement can only be proved with the condition $(x, y) \neq (0, 0)$, which is the one used below (it contains every matrix with $x \neq 0$; only the matrices with $x = 0$, $y \neq 0$ are added).

Let $P = \begin{pmatrix} x & y \\ -y & x \end{pmatrix}$ and $Q = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ -b & a \end{pmatrix}$ be in $G$.

**Closure.**
$$PQ = \begin{pmatrix} xa - yb & xb + ya \\ -ya - xb & -yb + xa \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} X & Y \\ -Y & X \end{pmatrix}, \quad X = xa - yb,\; Y = xb + ya,$$
which has the required form with real $X, Y$. Moreover
$$X^{2} + Y^{2} = (x^{2} + y^{2})(a^{2} + b^{2}) > 0,$$
so $(X, Y) \neq (0, 0)$ and $PQ \in G$.

**Identity.** $I = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ is of the required form ($x = 1$, $y = 0$) and $PI = IP = P$ for every $P$.

**Inverse.** $\det P = x^{2} + y^{2} \neq 0$, so
$$P^{-1} = \frac{1}{x^{2} + y^{2}}\begin{pmatrix} x & -y \\ y & x \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} x' & y' \\ -y' & x' \end{pmatrix}, \quad x' = \frac{x}{x^{2} + y^{2}},\; y' = \frac{-y}{x^{2} + y^{2}}.$$
This has the required form and $(x', y') \neq (0, 0)$, so $P^{-1} \in G$. (If $x \neq 0$ then $x' \neq 0$.)

**Associativity** is assumed (matrix multiplication is associative).

Closure, identity, inverses and associativity all hold, so $G$ is a group under matrix multiplication. $\blacksquare$

questions.enonce_markdown:
Solve the linear congruence
$$x - 3 \equiv 5 \pmod 7,$$
giving your answer in the form $x = p\mu + q$, where $p, q \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\mu \in \mathbb{Z}$. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Add $3$ to both sides (allowed in modular arithmetic):
$$x \equiv 5 + 3 = 8 \equiv 1 \pmod 7.$$
So $x$ leaves remainder $1$ on division by $7$:
$$\boxed{x = 7\mu + 1, \quad \mu \in \mathbb{Z}}$$
that is $p = 7$ and $q = 1$.

Check: for $\mu = 0$, $x = 1$ and $x - 3 = -2 \equiv 5 \pmod 7$ since $-2 + 7 = 5$. For $\mu = 1$, $x = 8$ and $x - 3 = 5$.
